newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's ANC denies U-turn on Mandela successor.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's ANC denies U-turn on Mandela successor.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela's party on Monday slapped down a newspaper report that he had disavowed Thabo Mbeki as his likely successor, calling it "superficial sensationalism signifying nothing".
The strong denial reflected South Africa's sensitivity to reports of potential political instability and the negative impact they might have on its immediate economic health.
Foreign exchange dealers said the banner headline had unnerved an already fragile rand, which at one point on Monday shed nearly two cents against the U.S. dollar.

Mbeki, deputy president and heir apparent to South Africa's first black leader, is on a mission to Europe to try to increase trade and investment. It is the latest in a series of high-profile foreign trips widely seen as grooming for his eventual succession.

The offending report, carried in Johannesburg's The Star daily, said Mandela had dropped a "bombshell" at the weekend, warning the executive of his ruling African National Congress (ANC) that he did not endorse Mbeki as its next leader and had said so in a weekend newspaper interview.
In the interview, with correspondents of the New York Times, The Times and Sowetan, Mandela had stressed that it was not up to him alone to choose the country's next leader.
He said it was a "misconception" that he had tapped Mbeki for the job, since that was the prerogative of the national executive committee of his party.

"The president has no right to choose a successor and I never did so. When the president of the ANC steps down, the National Executive Committee or congress will elect a successor," Mandela told his interviewers.
He added: "If (they) elect Mbeki, I will support that because he is a competent man who deserves that position."

Under a banner headline saying "Mandela drops Mbeki bombshell", the Star quoted an ANC executive source as saying "everyone was shocked" by Mandela's announcement, which the source said would trigger a race for the presidency.
This was hotly denied on Monday, both by the party executive and by a spokesman for Mandela.
"What he said is nothing new. He repeated what he has been saying all along, namely that he does not have the right to anoint a successor," spokesman Joel Netshitenzhe said.
The ANC said that rather than distance himself from Mbeki, Mandela had underlined his support for his deputy.
"If anything, President Mandela reiterated his vote of confidence in deputy president Thabo Mbeki," ANC spokesman Ronnie Mamoepa told Reuters.
In a tough statement, the ANC said: "The story in The Star is nothing but superficial sensationalism signifying nothing."
It confirmed that Mandela had indeed briefed the party's national executive on his newspaper interview, and how he underlined that ANC leaders are not anointed by him alone.

"Having said so, the president went further to indicate that should the constitutional structures of the ANC elect...Mbeki, the president would give such nomination his unqualified support," the ANC statement added.
Mandela, 78, constantly tries to reassure foreign investors that his retirement will not set the country dangerously adrift.
In his weekend interview he repeated his determination to step down as president in 1999, when general elections are due, to make way for younger blood.

Last July, Mandela gave a clear signal that he believed Mbeki was the best man to fill his shoes, saying: "He is very talented and very popular and if the organisation elected him I would feel they had made the right decision."
